scope.focus: Neurotechnology and neural engineering from first principles: how nervous-system signals arise, how they are measured and modulated, how neural interfaces and neuroprosthetic systems are engineered, and how biological, computational, device, clinical, regulatory, human-factors, and neuroethical constraints interact.
includes: Neuroanatomy and neurophysiology for engineers, from membranes, ions, action potentials, and synapses to populations, circuits, systems, and behavior

Neural recording across scales and modalities, including intracellular and extracellular electrophysiology, microelectrode arrays, ECoG/iEEG, EEG, peripheral nerve recordings, MEG, fMRI, and optical approaches

Electrode-tissue interfaces, bioinstrumentation, sampling, noise, artifacts, signal conditioning, neural data representation, spectral analysis, spike analysis, decoding, encoding, system identification, and machine learning

Electrical, magnetic, acoustic, optical, and other modulation approaches; deep brain stimulation, spinal and peripheral stimulation, noninvasive stimulation, closed-loop neuromodulation, and stimulation safety principles

Brain-computer interfaces, peripheral neural interfaces, sensory and motor neuroprostheses, bidirectional interfaces, assistive communication, restoration, rehabilitation, and augmentation as distinct design goals
Neural implant materials, biocompatibility, foreign-body response, flexible bioelectronics, packaging, power, telemetry, reliability, manufacturing, MRI/EMC considerations, and chronic performance
Neuroimaging, neural tissue engineering, regenerative interfaces, in-vitro neural platforms, multimodal neurotechnology, and computational models

Human-centered design, verification and validation, preclinical and clinical evidence, neurological-device regulation, cybersecurity, privacy, accessibility, equity, informed consent, agency, identity, and neuroethics
Research literacy, reproducibility, benchmark design, systems engineering, critical paper reading, computational reproduction, and frontier refreshes
delegates: General linear-algebra machinery may import explicit prerequisites from Linear Algebra when advanced decoding, dimensionality reduction, inverse problems, or state-space methods require it.

General machine-learning machinery may connect to the Large Language Models track only for shared mathematical or computational techniques; neural data claims remain grounded in neuroengineering evidence.
Advanced circuit, electromagnetic, and power-electronics derivations may import explicit support from Electrical Engineering — Power Engineering rather than silently assuming those skills.
Large software systems, embedded implementation, and low-level programming may import explicit support from C++, Computer Systems, or Linux when projects require them.
Normative analysis of agency, consent, identity, privacy, and responsibility may connect to Philosophy and Logic while keeping neurotechnology-specific empirical claims in this track.
